turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Howzit, Mr Naidoo. Come through, I'll do your obs quickly before Doctor Pillay sees you. You look a bit washed out, hey.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, sister, shame, I'm not lekker at all. The tummy's been hectic.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Arm straight for me, please. Blood pressure is one hundred and eight over seventy-two, and your pulse is ninety-six.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Temperature is thirty-seven point two, oxygen is ninety-eight percent, breathing sixteen a minute. Your lips are quite dry.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Afternoon, Mr Naidoo. Doctor Pillay. Sister's given me the numbers. What's brought you in?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The runs, doctor, and I was vomiting. It started after my cousin's wedding.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): A wedding meal. Do you know which day that was?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Last Saturday, or the Saturday before that? I can't hold the date in my head. Sometime recent, that's the best I can do.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the loose stools, did they start that same night or afterwards?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I think the next morning. Or maybe two days later. I really don't know, doctor. Dates are just gone.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the timing open then. How many times have you been to the loo?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish, I lost count. Maybe six, maybe ten. Watery, the whole day, nothing solid. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood, or mucus, that you actually saw?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. I didn't look properly. I don't know.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): So that's a maybe, not a yes. I won't write down blood in the stool. Tell me about the vomiting.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Three times the first night... no, it was four times that night. Then once yesterday morning, and nothing since. Sjoe.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vomiting has settled then. Was there any blood in what came up?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No blood. It was the chicken curry and the prawns, basically. Yoh, that prawn thing was rich.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did anyone else from the wedding get sick?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. My cousin, his wife, and I think two bridesmaids. Same thing, puking and the runs. So the whole table, almost.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, and the DJ played until late, the robot on the way home was out, we sat in the bakkie forever. Not important, I know.

[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud here. If several of you fell ill after the same meal, this is probably something in the food, a short-lived gastroenteritis, toxin or a virus, rather than one person catching flu. Cramps?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, low in the tummy, comes in waves. Worse just before I have to go, and it eases a bit once I've been.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Still nauseous?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit, ja. Not like the first day. I can sit here without feeling I'm going to bring up.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did you feel feverish, hot or cold shakes?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. A bit warm in the night, sometimes, not really. I don't know, doctor. I never checked.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then I won't call it a fever. The thermometer here is normal anyway. Dizzy at all?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): A little when I stand up fast. And I'm thirsty all the time, mouth like cotton.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Since the vomiting stopped, are you keeping water down?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Sort of. Small sips. I don't know how much I've managed, doctor. Some water, a bit of Coke. Not lekker amounts.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): What have you taken for it?

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Loperamide, the Imodium from the chemist. I took two milligrams... ag no, each tablet is two and I swallowed two of them by mouth, so four milligrams. Twice yesterday, and once this morning.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): And somebody told you not to?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): The sister at the chemist said if it's a bug, don't block it up, just drink. I took it anyway because I had to go to a thing and I couldn't be on the loo the whole time.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I understand the reason, but please stop the loperamide from now. If there's an infection we want it out, not held in. Any medicines you take every day?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, for the blood pressure. Five milligrams... no, sorry, it's ten milligrams. Every morning. Been on it for years.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): So high blood pressure, on ten milligrams each morning, as you've just said. Did you manage today's dose?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. This morning, by mouth, with a sip of water. That one I'm sure of.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies? Medicines, food?
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. My ma always said penicillin, but I can't remember what it did. No rash I can picture. Maybe, maybe not.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll note a possible penicillin allergy, uncertain, no clear reaction remembered. Operations in the past?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Never been cut open.

[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, they did bloods once. Last winter, or the winter before, I don't know which. They said my sugar was borderline. Just that word, borderline. No proper number that I remember.

[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): So a glucose test sometime back, reported to you as borderline, not a diagnosis, and we don't have a value. I won't treat that as confirmed. Any burning when you pass urine, or going more often?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No, urine's normal.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? Short of breath?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain, and I'm breathing fine.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright. Let me have a look. Mouth open. Ja, the tongue and the inside of the cheeks are dry.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Skin on the hand, it tents just a little and comes back slowly. Mild dehydration, I'd say, not severe.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tummy is soft. Mild tenderness in the middle, no guarding, and the bowel sounds are busy, which fits with the runs.

[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Putting it together, my working impression is acute gastroenteritis after that wedding meal, with the mild dehydration. I can't separate a food toxin from a short virus on the story alone, so that either-or is the differential, and I'm not calling food poisoning proven.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to send a stool test today. If the diarrhoea is no better in three days, or if you see clear blood, then we'll send a stool for microscopy and culture.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): For now, fluids. Small sips of oral rehydration, the sachets from the chemist, often, and water in between. Eat plain food if you're hungry, pap or toast, nothing rich.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the amlodipine going each morning, and stay off the loperamide. If the diarrhoea is no better in three days, or you can't keep fluids down, come back and see me.
[SEG0056] person_1 (NURSE): I'll fetch a Rehidrat sachet from the cupboard so you can start a glass here, and the chemist can sell you the box. Sip, don't gulp, hey.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Sharp, thank you. I don't know if I'll remember all of it, doctor, but I'll try the sips and I'll leave the Imodium.
[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's the main thing. If you feel faint, or you stop passing urine, don't wait the three days, come straight back or go to casualties.

spec.situation: Diarrhoea and vomiting after a trip or a wedding meal; others at the event are ill; patient counts bowel movements loosely; takes loperamide against advice; mild dehydration signs; stool test conditional; advice on fluids.
features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
